parts.title: Booking a walking holiday
parts.context: A man phones a travel company to ask about walking holidays.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a travel company to ask about walking holidays. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: jenny
script.text: Hillcrest Walking Holidays, Jenny speaking.

script.speaker: marco
script.text: Hello. I'd like some information about your walking holidays, please. A friend of mine went on one of your trips last year and recommended it.

script.speaker: jenny
script.text: That's good to hear. I'll take a few details first, and then I can tell you about our routes.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller heard about the company from a friend, so 'friend' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: jenny
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: marco
script.text: Yes, it's Marco Alvarez. That's A-L-V-A-R-E-Z.

script.speaker: jenny
script.text: Thank you, Mr Alvarez. And how many people would be in your group?

script.speaker: marco
script.text: There were going to be five of us, but one friend can't come now, so it's four.

script.speaker: jenny
script.text: That's fine. When would you like to travel?

script.speaker: marco
script.text: We're thinking of September, when the weather is cooler. We could only manage the first two weeks.

script.speaker: jenny
script.text: September is lovely. Now, would you prefer to stay in hotels or in smaller places?

script.speaker: marco
script.text: Smaller places, I think, preferably guesthouses. Hotels feel a bit impersonal.

script.speaker: jenny
script.text: We can arrange that. And how fit are you? How far do you usually walk in a day?

script.speaker: marco
script.text: We're not professionals, but we do about fifteen kilometres on a normal weekend walk.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: jenny
script.text: Let me tell you about our three routes. The Lakeside Trail is the easiest. It's twenty-two kilometres in total, and the path stays beside the water most of the way. You pass an old mill, which is now a café, so it's a good place to stop. It used to be sixty pounds a night, but the price went up this year, and it's now sixty-five.

script.speaker: marco
script.text: That sounds nice. What about something harder?

script.speaker: jenny
script.text: The High Ridge route is twenty-eight kilometres, with some steep climbs, and the views over the valley are spectacular. That one is eighty-two pounds a night.

script.speaker: marco
script.text: And the third?

script.speaker: jenny
script.text: Forest Way is forty-five kilometres, and it's mostly through woodland. You often see deer early in the morning, if you're quiet. It's fifty-eight pounds a night.

script.speaker: marco
script.text: Which would you recommend for people who walk fifteen kilometres at weekends?

script.speaker: jenny
script.text: I'd say the Lakeside Trail. You can do it comfortably in three days, and it's the best value, too.

script.speaker: marco
script.text: Then I'll talk to my friends and call you back. Thank you very much.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A visit to a cheese dairy
parts.context: The manager of a dairy talks to visitors before a tour.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a cheese dairy giving a talk to visitors. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: dennis
script.text: Good afternoon, everybody, and welcome to Hollin Dairy. I'm Dennis Whitaker, the manager. Before we start the tour, a little background. The farm has been in the family for two hundred years, but the cheese is newer. My great-grandfather started making it in nineteen twenty-six, so we've been doing it for almost a hundred years.

script.speaker: dennis
script.text: Our cows spend nine months of the year in the fields. Some farms do that to save money on feed, but for us the reason is flavour. The grass changes the taste of the milk, and you can taste the difference in the cheese.

script.speaker: dennis
script.text: Now, how do we make it? The milk comes straight from the milking parlour and is gently warmed. The first thing we add is a starter, which is a kind of friendly bacteria, and an hour later we add rennet, which makes the milk set. The solid part, called curd, is then cut and left to drain.

script.speaker: dennis
script.text: Most of our cheeses are ready after about three months, but the hard cheese called Old Barn is different. It's kept in the cold store for a full year, and some customers prefer it after two, but we don't sell it that old.

script.speaker: dennis
script.text: A word about hygiene. In the production area you'll need to wear a white coat and a hairnet, which you'll find on the hooks by the door. You don't need boots, because the floor is dry, and please don't bring any food in with you.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: dennis
script.text: Afterwards we'll go to the shop, where you can taste all five of our cheeses, and I'd like to tell you how to enjoy them at home.

script.speaker: dennis
script.text: Meadow White is our mildest cheese, and it's lovely crumbled into a salad. Old Barn is the strongest and the hardest. It's too dry for sandwiches, but it's perfect grated over pasta.

script.speaker: dennis
script.text: Blue Ridge, our blue cheese, is rich and salty, so many people like it with fruit, especially pears. Smoked Oak has a smoky flavour, which is wonderful melted on toast.

script.speaker: dennis
script.text: And finally Hollin Red, which is our bestseller. It's soft enough to spread, so it's the one to choose for a sandwich.

script.speaker: dennis
script.text: If you buy cheese today, it will keep for two weeks in the fridge. Wrap it in paper, not plastic, because cheese needs to breathe. And please do ask me any questions as we walk. If you'd like to follow me.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: An experiment on music and memory
parts.context: Two psychology students plan an experiment on music and memory.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two psychology students, Anna and Kofi, planning an experiment on music and memory. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Right, Kofi. We need to finalise the design of our experiment today. I've been wondering whether we should test memory or concentration.

script.speaker: kofi
script.text: I'd stick with memory. Concentration is much harder to measure, and Dr Lane said we should choose something we can score objectively.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: True. And for the music, I was thinking of pop, because that's what most students listen to while they study.

script.speaker: kofi
script.text: But pop has words, and words might get in the way of remembering words. Why don't we use music without singing?

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Good point. Classical it is. And we'll need a silent condition to compare it with.

script.speaker: kofi
script.text: How many participants do we need? Dr Lane said at least thirty.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: I'd prefer forty, twenty in each group, but we've only got two weeks, so thirty is realistic. That's fifteen in each group.

script.speaker: kofi
script.text: Fine. And where should we do it? The library's quiet, but we can't play music in there.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: We can book the psychology lab. It has headphones, so nobody else is disturbed, and a classroom would be far too noisy.

script.speaker: kofi
script.text: Good. What about the list of words? Twenty nouns?

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Twenty common nouns, yes, but we should avoid words that are related, like 'table' and 'chair', because people tend to remember them together.

script.speaker: kofi
script.text: Of course. I hadn't thought of that.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Now the procedure. First, we'll give everyone written instructions, so every participant gets exactly the same information, and a consent form to sign.

script.speaker: kofi
script.text: Then they put on headphones. In one group they hear the classical piece, and in the other group it's just silence.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: They'll have two minutes to study the list. We'll use a timer so it's exactly the same every time. I can use my phone.

script.speaker: kofi
script.text: Then should they do the test straight away?

script.speaker: anna
script.text: No. If we test them immediately they'll just repeat the words in their heads, so we'll give them a five-minute break first, and ask them to do a puzzle.

script.speaker: kofi
script.text: And the test is writing down all the words they can remember?

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Yes, in any order, and we'll count how many they get right. Then we compare the scores of the two groups to see whether the music made a difference.

script.speaker: kofi
script.text: Let's hope it did, or our results will be boring.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Even no difference is a result, Kofi. Dr Lane said so.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: how bats find their way
parts.context: A biology lecture on echolocation in bats.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how bats find their way. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly, and about one in five of all mammal species is a bat. Most of them hunt at night, which raises an obvious question: how do they find their way in the dark?

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The answer is echolocation. A bat makes a sound that is too high for humans to hear, and listens to the echo that comes back from the objects around it. From the delay of the echo, the bat can work out how far away something is, and from the quality of the echo it can tell what the object is.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The sounds are made in the larynx, or voice box, and in most species they come out of the mouth. But horseshoe bats send their calls out through the nose, which has a strange leaf-shaped structure that helps to focus the sound into a narrow beam.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Echolocation is extremely precise. A bat can detect a wire as thin as a human hair, and a small bat can catch hundreds of insects in an hour. As it gets close to its prey, the calls become much faster, until they form what is called a feeding buzz, of up to two hundred calls a second.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: But some insects have evolved defences. Tiger moths, for example, can hear the bat's calls, and they respond by producing clicking sounds of their own, which seem to confuse the bat and make it miss.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Not all bats use echolocation. Fruit bats, which feed on fruit and nectar, mostly rely on their large eyes and a very good sense of smell to find food.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Bats are also important to people. Many plants depend on them to carry their pollen, including the agave, which is used to make tequila. And their droppings, called guano, have been collected for centuries and used as fertiliser.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Sadly, many bat species are now under threat, from the loss of the places where they roost, and from diseases. So the next time you see a bat at dusk, remember how much they do for us. Next week, we'll look at owls.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
